Q1: Dispatch the medic to Call A (Maple St, 7.8) — the chest pain call. It is the highest-scored waiting call, and 7.8 means serious and needing a unit soon. Holding a medic idle while a cardiac call waits, merely because no call hit 9.0, would cost lives; the threshold triggers escalation, not dispatch.
Q2: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Pine Rd, 8.4) — the kitchen fire. It outranks the dumpster fire at 7.9, and a structure fire with people displaced is the higher urgency. Below 9.0 I dispatch without mutual aid or command notification; I do not hold the engine waiting for a critical call.
Q3: Dispatch the ladder to Call A (1st St, 8.9) — the reported trapped person with smoke showing. It edges Call B (8.8), and a possible trapped occupant beats an elevator rescue where occupants are not in immediate fire danger. Both sit just below 9.0, so no escalation — but the highest scorer still gets the unit, no holding.
Q4: Dispatch the BLS unit to Call A (Hill Rd, 7.1) — the diabetic emergency. A conscious diabetic patient can deteriorate fast, so 7.1 wins over a 5.5 event standby. Holding the BLS unit for a hypothetical worse call while a real patient waits is exactly the naive default the principle rejects.
Q5: Dispatch the medic to Call A (River St, 8.1) — the difficulty breathing call. The near-tie with Call B (8.0) is resolved by the score itself, and respiratory compromise carries the sharper time risk. Neither reaches 9.0, so no escalation — but the highest scorer gets the next unit, every time.
Q6: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Main St, 6.8) — the vehicle fire, and accept the neighboring jurisdiction's mutual aid offer for Call B (Side St, 6.5) — the brush fire near homes. Highest urgency wins my unit; the offered aid covers the second call rather than leaving it unanswered. Holding my engine while both burn would be indefensible.
Q7: Dispatch the battalion chief to Call A (Park Ave, 7.5) — the multi-vehicle accident needing command oversight. It is the only waiting call, and 7.5 is a genuine command need, not a borderline one. Holding command staff idle with an accident awaiting oversight gains nothing.
Q8: Dispatch the medic to Call A (Cedar Ln, 8.7) — the stroke symptoms with a closing treatment window. It is the clear highest scorer, and stroke is time-critical in a way abdominal pain is not. No escalation since it is below 9.0 — but it still gets the unit now, not after some arbitrary threshold.
Q9: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Summit Dr, 5.9) — the gas leak report. It is the only call in the queue, the home is evacuated, and a gas leak is a legitimate engine call regardless of score. Holding an idle engine for a higher-scoring future call while a gas leak waits is the naive default the principle forbids.
